Anna is an environmentalist and is studying the impact of deforestation in a pine forest located in a square-shaped region. Anna discovers that the area of ​​the deforested region is decreasing at a rate of $0.4{\text{ km}}^{2}/\text{month}.$ At what rate are the region's diagonals decreasing if the diagonals are $20\text{ km}$ long?

feedback.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14095797/assets/3518e235844a154f6fd680edd2a169d4ff3b9812dcc38bb86b658bfc6c5d6e35.png)

One of the panels is melted in a squared container and shrank in a way such that the area of the square decreases at a rate of $14\,{\text{m}}^{2}\text{/min}.$ At what rate are the diagonals of the square decreasing when the diagonals are $7\,\text{m}$ each?
feedback.worked_solution:
Let $h$ and $A$ be the length of the diagonals and the area of the square, respectively. Using the Pythagorean theorem, it can be shown that the relationship between $A$ and $h$ is

$$
A=\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}.
$$

We want to find

$$
\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}h}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot h \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{h}\cdot \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $A$ decreases at a rate of $14\,{\text{m}}^{2}\text{/min},$ so

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =-14.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we want to compute the rate of change of the diagonals when the diagonal has length $h=7.$ Substituting this information into our expression for $\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{7}\cdot (-14) \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-2\text{ m}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the diagonals of the square are decreasing at a rate of $2\text{ m}\text{/min}.$
